tip: To take a class or course, Portuguese uses 'fazer' (to do), not 'tomar': 'fazendo um curso' = taking a course.
'Por que' (two words, no accent) = why (in questions). 'Porque' (one word) = because (in answers).
In questions, 'por que' is two words; the joined 'porque' answers them: 'Por que você não veio?' = why didn't you come?
In speech Brazilians use 'tem' for 'there is': 'tem uma farmácia' means 'there's a pharmacy'. The textbook 'há' sounds formal.
Personality traits use 'ser' – they're part of who you are: 'é muito gentil' = he's very kind (inherently).
'Estar bonita/linda' = she looks beautiful right now. 'Ser bonita/linda' = she is beautiful in general. Both are compliments but with different nuances.
'Onde' = where. 'Aonde' = where to (with motion verbs): 'aonde você vai?'
Clock times use 'às': 'às dez' = at ten. It is 'a' plus feminine 'as', since hours are feminine ('as horas').
'Dar conta de' means to handle or manage something: 'ela dá conta de tudo.' Literally 'to give account of.'
'Perguntar' is to ask a question. To ask for something is 'pedir.' Here: 'perguntar para o garçom,' ask the waiter.
Regular '-er' verbs in the past drop '-er' and add '-eu' for he/she/you: 'comer' becomes 'comeu' (ate).
'Ao' is the preposition 'a' fused with 'o': 'vamos ao cinema' means 'we go to the cinema'.
Transport uses 'ir de': 'vai de Uber' = goes by Uber. Use 'de' for car, bus, or train; 'a pé' (on foot) is an exception.
After a feeling noun, use 'de' before the verb: 'vergonha de falar' (embarrassed to speak), 'medo de cair' (afraid to fall).
Event locations use 'ser': 'a festa é na casa' = the party takes place at the house. This is about where the event happens, not where something is located.
'De' + 'o' contracts to 'do': 'típico do Nordeste' (typical of the Northeast). They don't normally stay apart as 'de o'.
'Sem' plus an infinitive equals English 'without' plus -ing: 'sem pensar' = without thinking.
'Dar certo' is literally 'to give right' and means to work out: 'vai dar certo' says 'it is going to work out'.
In Brazil 'chegar' (to arrive) takes 'em': 'chego na rodoviária' ('na' = 'em' + 'a'). Formal or European usage prefers 'chegar a'.
'Por que' in two words asks a question; 'porque' in one word means because: 'Por que o preço subiu?'
'Ser' for identity, 'estar' for the moment: 'é advogada' says what she is, 'está trabalhando' what she is doing right now.
Marital status normally uses 'ser', not 'estar', even though it can change: 'ele é solteiro', 'ela é casada'.
'Ligar' takes 'para', not a direct object: 'ligou para você' = 'called you'. You call to someone in Portuguese.
'Pronto para' + an infinitive means ready to do something: 'pronto para sair' (ready to leave).
'Estar' marks a changed condition, so spoiled milk is 'o leite está estragado', not 'é estragado'.
In Brazil 'você' (you) often pairs with 'te' for the object: 'quem te contou' (who told you), mixing 'você' with the older 'te'.
'O que tem' is an extremely casual and common way to ask what's available. Literally 'what does it have.'
'Como se chama' literally means 'how does it call itself.' Use it for things and people: 'como se chama esse prato?' or 'como você se chama?'
Even though pregnancy is temporary, 'estar grávida' is the standard expression – never use 'ser grávida'.
Portuguese uses 'qual é' where English says 'what is', to single one out: 'qual é a sua comida favorita?'
